summary: Defines MZAP, a protocol for discovering the multicast administrative scope zones relevant at a particular location. It was a standards-track document, and its status is now historic.

eli5.summary: Group broadcasts have borders. MZAP tells a place which borders it sits inside. It is now historic.

questions: how to discover multicast scope zones
subtitle: A protocol to discover multicast administrative scope zones and detect router misconfigurations.

tldr.problem: Networks use administrative scope zones to control multicast broadcast boundaries, but have no way to discover which zones exist locally or to detect when routers are misconfigured.
tldr.mechanism: MZAP defines four message types that routers send to announce scope zones, check that zone boundaries form convex regions, detect leaks, and report nesting relationships.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Historic; multicast scoping has largely been superseded by other technologies, though the mechanisms remain relevant for administrators managing legacy systems.

today: RFC 2365 is a Historic document. Administratively-scoped multicast has not become standard practice on the Internet. MZAP remains a complete, valid specification for organizations that deploy multicast scoping internally.

sections.title: The Problem of Scope Discovery
sections.content:
When networks use administratively-scoped IP multicast as defined in RFC 2365, they divide multicast addresses into ranges, each confined to a specific area by boundary routers. For example, 239.192/14 might be reserved for a corporate intranet, ensuring that broadcasts stay within the company. Applications and services running inside these zones need to know what zones exist, their address ranges, and their names, but until MZAP, no protocol existed to discover this information dynamically.

The RFC identifies two practical barriers: applications cannot discover scope zones automatically, and router misconfiguration is easy to miss. A zone might be non-convex (packets traveling between two nodes in the zone pass outside it), or leaky (boundaries not fully configured), or conflicting (overlapping addresses). Administrators had no way to detect these problems.
sections.eli5: Broadcast borders are invisible. MZAP lets a machine see which borders are nearby and tells the manager if a border is broken.

sections.title: Scope Zones and Boundaries
sections.content:
A multicast scope zone is an area of the network topology enclosed by one or more scope boundaries on router interfaces. These boundaries prevent multicast packets in a particular address range from crossing. A Zone Boundary Router (ZBR) is a router configured with such a boundary.

The simplest scope is the Local Scope, defined in RFC 2365 as 239.255.0.0/16 for IPv4. Every ZBR must have a Local Scope boundary on every interface that has any other scope boundary. Organizations can create additional, nested zones; for instance, a building-wide zone inside a campus-wide zone inside a company-wide zone.

A Zone ID is the lowest IP address used by any ZBR in a zone to send MZAP messages into that zone. The combination of the Zone ID and the multicast address range uniquely identifies a zone, even if the same address range is reused in different parts of the network.
sections.eli5: A border router sits at a broadcast border and knows about it. The Zone ID is like the lowest-numbered router standing guard at the border.

sections.title: Zone Announcement and Discovery
sections.content:
ZBRs send Zone Announcement Messages (ZAMs) periodically (every 10 minutes by default) to the well-known multicast address 239.255.255.252 (the Local Scope address). A ZAM contains the scope's address range, Zone ID, and human-readable names in multiple languages. Any host—including address allocators and multicast directory servers—can listen for these messages to learn what zones exist locally.

ZAMs are also forwarded across Local Scope boundaries within the larger scope zone, so all Local Scope regions inside a scope zone eventually learn of its existence. When a ZBR receives a ZAM, it may forward it to other Local Scope zones (except the one it came from), with timing duplication suppression to prevent flooding.

To discover nesting relationships between zones, ZBRs send Not-Inside Messages (NIMs), which state that one zone does not nest inside another. By collecting these negations, servers can deduce which zones are nested (if no evidence of non-nesting accumulates, nesting is presumed).
sections.eli5: Border routers shout out descriptions of their zones every 10 minutes. Other parts of the network hear these shouts and learn which borders they are inside. Routers also say when one border is definitely not inside another.

sections.title: Detecting Misconfigurations
sections.content:
MZAP includes mechanisms to detect four classes of misconfiguration:

Non-convex zones: Zone Convexity Messages (ZCMs) allow ZBRs to compare notes about which other ZBRs they can see. If a ZBR hears about another ZBR in a ZCM but cannot reach it (according to the multicast routing table), the zone is non-convex.

Leaky boundaries: If a ZAM originates inside a scope zone and arrives on an interface outside the zone, it has leaked through a misconfigured boundary. The originating router sends Zone Limit Exceeded (ZLE) messages if a ZAM travels through too many Local Scope zones; this detects leaks where packets reach distant parts of the network.

Leaky Local Scope: If a ZBR receives a ZAM and the Zone ID reported differs from its own Zone ID for that scope, the Local Scope itself is leaky (a boundary is missing on some interface).

Conflicting ranges: If a ZBR receives a ZAM whose address range overlaps but does not match a locally-configured range, the ranges conflict. Similarly, if a name for a scope differs between received and local configurations, the names conflict.
sections.eli5: MZAP checks four broken setups: borders that leave holes, messages leaking out and back, Local Scope not sealed, and mismatched settings. The router logs each problem so the network manager can fix it.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
All MZAP messages are sent over UDP to port 2106 with a TTL of 255. Each message begins with a common header containing a version field (0), a "Big" scope bit indicating whether address allocators can use the entire range, a packet type (0-3), address family (IPv4 or IPv6), and the count of zone names.

The header is followed by addresses for the message origin, Zone ID, and the scope zone's start and end addresses. Zone names are encoded with language tags and flags, supporting multiple names in different languages, all padded to 4-byte boundaries.

The four message types differ in their payloads: ZAMs carry zones traveled information and a path list; ZLEs copy the ZAM that triggered them; ZCMs list the addresses of nearby ZBRs; NIMs reference a second scope zone's address range to declare non-nesting.
sections.eli5: All four message types follow the same format: header, addresses, and optional details. They travel as UDP packets with a high TTL so they reach far into the zone.

sections.title: Status and Deployment
sections.content:
RFC 2776 is a Historic Internet Standard. While the protocol was technically sound, multicast scoping itself has not been widely deployed in the broader Internet due to operational complexity and the popularity of alternative approaches (such as VLAN-based isolation and application-level group management). Consequently, MZAP is rarely encountered in modern deployments, though it remains relevant for organizations that have implemented administratively-scoped multicast for internal use.

The RFC documents a complete solution to the scope discovery and configuration validation problem, and the message formats and algorithms remain valid for anyone implementing multicast scope management.
sections.eli5: The protocol is complete and correct, but multicast borders were not widely used on the Internet. It is still useful for companies that set up these borders internally.
